samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Herbert Shure was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: I was drafted. I received -- I was in college at the time and I was studying engineering and I received three deferments because I was in school. But I was in an area where there weren't very many draftable age fellows, most of who were available were in college or out of town, and they said that my -- the limit that they had for deferment, whether it's right or not, they told me they could only give three and I would have to go. Besides, they said to me, why don't you spend the year in the Army and get it over with and then you can finish up with college and you might get some financing from the government, which I never even sought, but until the G.I. Bill of Rights came out. But, they did take me and that was in -- July 3, the day before the 4th of July in 1941. And the group that I was drafted with from Cleveland, when we gathered and were sworn in at the old armory the corner of Sixth and Lakeside -- am I doing all right? I don't want to go on and on.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No, no. This is what we want. Exactly.

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: We gathered at the Armory and there must have been 100 of us or 150. I don't know. I am not good at numbers, with judging crowds, but there were perhaps 150 of us. And we marched from the Armory to the Terminal Tower at about 6:30 and everyone was leaving downtown. Maybe it was a little earlier than that. Perhaps around 5:30. And we got on a train and got to Fort Hayes in Columbus about 8:00 o'clock that night. And we occupied a whole floor in one of the barracks there at Fort Hayes. And in the morning, early in the morning, we were issued uniforms and I -- they ran out of shirts. They weren't very well organized, I didn't think, but they ran out of shirts and gave me a World War I shirt which I had to put over my head and it was like wool. It was a different material. Everyone else was getting cotton, and I had this wool shirt for about two days. And then they finally got another shipment of shirts and fitted me right. But it was such a new experience. I remember saluting a Salvation Army guy and he had a choke collar and buttons all the way down his front, and he had this blue tunic, and I saluted him and he laughed and said, "I am not in your Army, I am a different Army. I am in God's Army", he said. Anyway, that was one of the first boo-boos I made, and although over the years I made a lot of them. Almost everyone that I was shipped down to Fort Hayes with moved out in about two days, two or three days, and they all went to the Medical Corps in Virginia and about eight of us were left, all of us on this large barracks room full of beds. And there were only eight of us and we went to the engineers at Fort Bellford and we had basic training, and it was a brand new training center. It wasn't even completed yet. And we were the second group to arrive there. And we were, the eight of us, were mixed in with hundreds of others, and we were there for about -- I think we were there for three months. In the end of September, we were supposed to be well trained and we were shipped to Hawaii. Now, they told us -- or we didn't know where we were going, but there were 1200 of us and they split us up into three groups, and we took three trains. There were three trains. One went the northern route, the northern Pacific; one went right down the center of the country; and the group I was with went south to Georgia and across the gulf states, and we came into Texas at the gulf and went diagonally across to Albuquerque. It took us three days to get out of Texas, and we would stop for hours at a time to let other trains that had priorities, I guess, but I think everything was scheduled so that the three trains arrived at Fort Mason, and we didn't know we were going there, but the last day as we were going through a pass in California, this civilian who was there with us -- and became very friendly with us and was talking, he said you guys are going to Fort Mason. And I had looked on a map because I knew we were in California, and I thought we were going to Fort Ord or some place like that, or Persidio (phonetic), I was hoping. When they said Fort Mason, I found it. It was in San Francisco, and I thought how lucky we are to be in San Francisco. But Fort Mason was just a dock. And the trains pulled in one behind another. Talk about logistics. And we all debarked and got on this boat. It was the Satan Hill. It had been a present line boat -- ship, I guess, rather than a boat. I guess it was a ship. And the name was changed to Satan Hill. And we sailed out by sunset. We were just leaving San Francisco. We passed under the Golden Gate, and that was quite a thrill. We were all out on deck shouting and waving whatever we had to wave, and we went out into the Pacific, and I think it took us a week to sail. We didn't know where we were going, but we ended up in Honolulu at the Aloha Tower. And we were taken by train, by a little dinky-tinky train. It was only -- the tracks were only about two feet wide, apart. And it was really, I think, a plantation or sugar cane plantation train. They took us up to Scofield barracks. Now, when we got there and were debarking, I didn't know anyone in the Army, but at the bottom of this gangplank that we had to walk down into this large kind of a large shed, the fellow standing there was an old friend of mine. I mean, we were in school together. He had an appointment to West Point and he was a lieutenant in this engineering regiment. We were recommissioned that September, and we formed the 34th Engineers. It was decommissioned after the first World War and they were just recommissioning it. There were 1200 of us draftees, but the cadre were made up of experienced non-coms from the 3rd Engineers. The 3rd Engineers were stationed -- that was their headquarters there in Scofield barracks. But apparently they had taken one battalion of 3rd Engineers and they shipped them to the Philippines. They were in Corregidor. And they broke up the 2nd Battalion. I don't know if it was -- they broke it up entirely or not, but those who were left of the 2nd Battalion for the most part made up three different regiments, the 65th who were combat engineers; the 34th, we were construction; and then another engineering regiment, and we didn't get in contact with them at all. I guess they were at Scofield, but they were in aviation regiment who were to build airfields, and we were all there on kind of training missions, I guess. But we didn't have any equipment. We borrowed equipment from contractors after the war started. I guess we just took them, commanded their trucks and bulldozers and all the things we needed, cement mixers. We had so many cement mixers. I don't know where they got them all. I think they scrounged from other regiments. But being construction engineers, we were on detached service at Ulu Po Heiau (phonetic) peninsula which was part of Kaneohe Bay, and it was -- we were building the coast artillery camp and gun emplacements along the entire east coast of Oahu, and we had almost completed the construction of the camp. We were using some of the barracks that we built and the mess hall that we had built, but it wasn't entirely completed. And it was part of the Naval Reservation. It was located about midway between Bellows Field, which was to the south of us, and Kaneohe Bay Naval Air Station, which was just to the north, but we were closer to them than to Bellows. And I know that when the war started, when Pearl Harbor was attacked, we were attacked at the same time, and the two raids really demolished both the facilities at Bellows Field and at the Naval Air Station. The Naval Air Station was really hit badly. And just as a side line, we were told that on Thursday before the attack, they had transferred fuel oil out of one tank. They had three underground tanks. They had transferred fuel oil to the two other tanks and the one was empty. And when they attacked Kaneohe, they struck and set on fire the two underground tanks that had gasoline fuel in them. And the third tank that was empty wasn't even bombed. But they destroyed the hangar. And there were 36 planes stationed at Kaneohe. They were all PVYs, patrol planes that would take off every single day and patrol that central part of the Pacific. Out of the 36, only three were left. They got 33. The three left were out on patrol, but they apparently were patrolling south of Hawaii and not north, or they would have been able to intercept that attacking force which was about 250 miles north of Oahu. Anyway, when we were attacked, I was having breakfast with a friend of mine, Mike Foster, and of all the men drafted, I think he was -- he was given a position that was most suitable for him. He was not, what you might call, a military type. He was an artist, a very sensitive guy, and very well educated, and they put him to head up a camouflage unit and that is what he was doing. He was really in the headquarter company. We were the D Company and he was sent to us to start camouflaging some of the things we were working on. I don't remember precisely what it was. But I hadn't seen him for several weeks, and we were pretty good friends because we were both from Cleveland. He graduated from the Cleveland School of Art. But other than that, we had a lot in common and we were pretty good friends. Anyway, we had been together through basic training. We were in the same squad and we were only parted when he went to headquarters company and I was in Company D. But he was with us for a couple of weeks and we were having breakfast together almost every day. And on this particular Sunday, we were eating. We had scrambled eggs and, I guess, bacon or sausage, and he passed me a fresh bottle of ketchup and he said, "Come on, put it on your eggs. It will taste better. They are awfully dry." Well, he always used ketchup on his scrambled eggs. We had scrambled eggs frequently. But I wasn't in the mood to argue or resist, and I opened up the bottle and it was just a new bottle and nothing came out. And I kept shaking and pumping it, and finally I hit the bottom of the bottle, and it was upside down and almost the whole contents of bottle splashed on to my scrambled eggs. And just as it hit the plate or hit the eggs, the table and plate and everything came up in the air. It almost -- it came up so high that it was almost chin high. And I thought what the hell did I do. And I looked into the bottle to see if there was something there that was explosive, and of course there was this awful explosion. The whole building shook. And I remember we had a wreck. This was at the mess hall. It was just a temporary building really. I am sure it no longer exists. It was all frame and it was jerry-built, really. But we had racks on the wall, hanging on the wall. They put the dishes in there to dry because they air dried dishes and they all fell onto the floor, I mean the ground. Not ground, but it was a concrete. No, it wasn't concrete floor. It was a wooden floor. But they all came clashing down. And I couldn't understand it. And then everybody started running. And we ran to the back and out the back door, and we -- and the first thing I saw was flames rising, flames of black smoke coming from the air station, and planes were strafing us. But I didn't know they were strafing. There were just a couple that had passed rather low. And Mike and I ran out and behind the mess hall there was a latrine, a toilet building. And it had a rather low roof. And I hoisted him up onto the roof and somebody else hoisted me up, and we got on the roof of the latrine to get a better view of what was going on at Kaneohe, at the Naval Air Station. And here we saw dive bombers hitting the hangar and explosions and noise and oh, my. And then this plane came strafing us, and he kind of banked the plane a little bit so that he could line up with Bellows Field, and I saw the pilot and I waved at him. And then I noticed this huge disk, this orange disk on the side off the fuselage and realized that we were attacked by the Japanese. It was terrible. So we watched these firing, strafing us, and there was little clouds of dust that the bullets were picking up, and he missed all of us. Well, we lost one man that day. And he was unlucky. He was killed. But the rest of us, we assembled, the bugle blew for call to arms, I guess, or to assemble, and we all got together and got the rifles. We weren't much of a fighting group, but we did go back to the barracks and get our rifles and marched to the Naval Air Station because the captain said they are going to need us there. If there is an invasion, they are going to need us there. So we went to the Naval Air Station, and so the war began for us. Well, what happened to me was, like everyone else, we were doing construction work, and I would take my shirt shirt off, and we wore what we call Panama hats to protect us from the sun, but they weren't much protection. And the first nine months I was there, I lost four layers of skin. I got so sunburned. We had a regiment picture taken or company picture taken at Ulu Po Heiau. It was this little peninsula. Actually, it was kind an island that was connected to the mainland with a causeway, and the causeway had a guard station about halfway across. And I remember after the war started, about three days after the war started, the Marines drove a herd of cattle on to the Ulu Po Heiau peninsula. In the event we were cut off, we would have beef on hoof, I guess. But there was, oddly enough, there was a bird farm, a pheasant farm, just adjacent to where we were building this camp. And they were raising pheasants for the hotels in Honolulu. And they decided to kill them all. I don't know who did that. I think it must have been the Navy. They killed 400 pheasants and they ate some of them, and we ate. I had four of them. They are little things, but they are delicious. But they prepared the pheasants and that must have been the first week of the war. And we didn't have too much food. We weren't getting food. I remember for breakfast one day, the only thing we had was canned fruit cocktail, Del Monte fruit cocktail. I think I was on K.P. duty that day. You can eat as much as you want to. But that is the sort of thing we went through for the first week or two, but after that, everything was very well organized. What else can I tell you?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What was your specific job?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Well, I started out, of course, I was just a plain private, and started out as part of a work crew, but then when they discovered I had some engineering background, they gave me a transit and a level and I was doing surveying. And after I had lost four lawyers of skin, I just pealed like a bird, I guess. And they put me on a desk job, but the desk job was still in surveying topographical squad, and we were chaining roads and running -- we were running various projects. We were doing the surveying. One thing that we worked on for several weeks was laying out a test site for anti-aircraft guns -- not anti-aircraft, anti-tank guns. And it was a tank that -- we had a track the tanks were moving on. I guess they were being pulled by a truck with a long rope and the squads were shooting at the tank. That was one of the last projects that I worked on, because after -- let's see. We were attacked in December. The following October, I had been on the island a month -- a year and a month. I transferred to the Air Force. I was gung-ho to be a pilot because when we were being attacked, when the second attack came, three V-17s were flown in from the states. They were stripped down. They didn't have any armament at all. But they arrived at Bellows. I don't think that was their destination. They were probably going to Hickam. But they were trying to land at Bellows while Bellows was under attack. Isn't that awful. And all three were shot down. And I saw that. I saw one plane that came down somewhere around Kailua and hit the ground and went into flames, and I think there must have been a crew of perhaps three that were killed. But during the first attack at Bellows, a couple of pilots got into -- they had B-40's there, and two of them started -- they took off. They got to the end of the runway and along came a jet plane and it just shot down. They didn't even get up in the air. And just witnessing that, I decided that that is where I wanted to be. I wanted to get to the Air Force and be a pilot. So I signed up, and they almost immediately took me. I was tested for almost a full day, given intelligence tests and physical tests. And I passed everything. And I was told that I would be called up in a few months, and that was, I think, in October. And in the beginning of November, I was transferred in the Air Force. And I went to Hickham Field where we were to board a troop transport back to the states for training. And the war in Guadalcanal was going on and the Navy took the ship we were supposed to be taking back to the states on. They took it to transport additional troops, or I think they made it into a hospital ship. But I don't know what happened to it. We weren't shipped out. And we were left at Hickham waiting for another ship. It didn't come in until the end of December. And we got to the states -- we got to the states the last week in December, so we must have left Hawaii about the middle of December, and we were escorted by two destroyers -- this was a slow ship -- and got to San Francisco where we were -- we were disembarked at Angel Island and we had to be on that island for a week for quarantine, so we didn't mix with the population and spread any tropical disease we were bringing. And after a week we got on a train and went south to Santa Ana where I was to get basic training for the Air Force. But they weren't ready for us yet. And we got down there on the first of January, the night of the first of January. And I think there were 400 of us. We were given a ten-day furlough. We went home. And I hadn't been home since I was drafted. When I got home, I had discovered my father was ill, and he was kind of waiting for me, and I was home a little less than a week and he died. So I remained for his funeral and I called my company commander in Santa Ana and asked if I could have additional time, and told him what happened. And he said yes, he said take another -- I forget. I think he gave me another week. So I took four days to get back by train. In any case, he was awfully nice to me. And I know the guy was some kind of character. He was a very handsome man, but he was a Hollywood character. His place was --- the place was loaded with Hollywood dogs. We had huge dogs there that people couldn't afford to keep and feed. They couldn't get the meat. So they gave them or loaned them as secure -- for security, I guess, because we used to have to patrol at Santa Ana at night. And we would walk with -- I recall walking with a Saint Bernard who was bigger than I was. Anyway, I washed out of flight training, and I was to be sent to the University of Chicago to study meteorology, and I remained in the Air Force as a weatherman. All that aside -- well, in any case, I was in the states for a year and then shipped to Britain. And the island was being loaded up with American forces and material, and you can't imagine the armaments that were shipped to that little island. I had, on several occasions, flew from Scotland into London. And it's amazing the people's back yards. There would be tanks lined up in them with tarpaulins over them and garages that were loaded with ammunition, and it was just everywhere. Anyway, I was stationed at Prestwick in Scotland, which was the terminus for the Air, ATC, Air Transport Command. All the freight that came in came in by air through Prestwick. They had the best weather in the British Isles. And so that was a very important station and we were the largest weather station that the Air Force had, I guess. We had satellite stations in the North Atlantic, and we were the -- we were the group. And most of the work I was doing was in deciphering and enciphering codes. We were the transfer point between the U.S. Air Force Weather Bureau or the U.S. Weather Bureau and and the Air Force weather stations and the British. We received signals from Washington that was a ____ and that came only once a day, about 6:00 o'clock. And we deciphered that code and then put it into the British code. And they have a very good code. Much better than ours. And then we transferred the weather data to the British and it required two men to walk from our station, which was housed on a mansion house overlooking this golf course in Prestwick called Red Bird, and the British had a similar large house adjacent -- about half a mile away, down a little country lane, and their place was called Red Bray (phonetic) and because we would walk over and hand them our material and they would do the same with theirs. Now, they gave us information from Europe, all of Scandinavia, and even Germany, and the Soviet Union and North Africa. And we gave them the rest of the world. We gave them all of Asia, North and South America, Southern -- or most of Africa except North Africa, and Australia, too, I believe, although I don't remember that very precisely anymore. But in any case, we transferred information. And among other things, there was a squadron of Norwegian pilots who were supplying the underground in Norway. It was headed up by a guy whose name was Belchin (phonetic). I will never forget him. He was an Arctic flyer. Probably the most experienced Arctic flyer in the world. He headed up that group. They had seven planes. And when they came in for briefing before a mission, MP's surrounded the building. No one was permitted in or out, and we couldn't go in the building. If we were outside the building, we couldn't go in until they left. If we were in, we were confined to our own station. We couldn't go into where they were being briefed. The security was very tight. And after I had been there a couple of months, they had a mission in which seven planes took off, and only two came back. Somebody had tipped the Germans off, and they just -- they moved out of Prestwick. They went up to Larakin in the Shetlands, and I don't know what happened to them after that and I don't even know if Belchin survived, but they sure were a nice bunch. Anyway, I met my wife Ishbell (phonetic) while I was stationed in Prestwick. She lived in the Martin which was close to Lockloman and we met on New Year's Eve. Although she wasn't my date -- I had someone else who I really neglected. I was attracted to her. She was classified as a British war bride. And after she -- we weren't married in Britain. I left and came back to the states. I had been overseas so long that I had a very high order number for coming back to the states or leaving the E.T.O., and I came back in -- I think it was June of '45. Just after the war ended in Europe. Then in May -- and I think it was the first week in June, that I was shipped out of E.T.O. and I don't know if I should go into all of this in detail. Am I doing all right?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You are doing great. You arrived in England probably in early '44, in Great Britain?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: In February of '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: And I met Ishbell on December the 31st of '44.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So go ahead and tell me what you were going to tell me.

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Well, I was transferred from Prestwick to an island in Wales. It was in the Irish Ocean, Irish Sea, and it was -- we called it Anglia -- and I think it was called the Island of Anglia. And we had an airfield there and there were so many planes in Britain they were shipping them back to the states just to get rid of them. And I worked at this station there for about a month and then I was shipped back to the states. However, when I came -- well, we were sent up to Warrington where there were acres of bombers and some of them were bombers that had been damaged in raids over Europe and couldn't get back to Britain. And so they went on and landed in a neutral country in Sweden, and there were hundreds of them in Sweden. And they entered the crew, but the crew had nothing to do, so they repaired. What they did was whatever planes were the least damaged, they repaired them from parts taken from other planes, salvage parts, and they sent back to Britain, I think it was 141 planes, and they were lined up in Ballington -- not Ballington, that was in London -- but it was Warrenton. And there were 11 of us assigned to this one plane and we were coming back to the states. It was a B-24 and a colonel was to be our pilot, and the 11 enlisted men, pilot, co-pilot and navigator and radio man, so that would have been 16 of us. Eleven -- yes. We were to come back on this plane and the colonel went up to the plane and kicked the tire and said, "I am not going to take this coffin home." He said, I am going to -- it's not, it's not flyable. I don't know how they got it here. And he left us. And we were standing around waiting and waiting. And finally a lieutenant came up and said "I am your new pilot, and we are flying back to the states." Well, we all got in the plane and we took off and we landed in Anglia. I don't have that word correct. I think we called it Anglie. Anyway, we landed at this airfield where I had been stationed for about a month, and the guys there were glad to see me and they said well, "You make up the flight plan as long as you are here, we are busy." And using the maps they had there, it showed there would be a front arriving in southern England in the morning and the weather would be fine all the way there. We were headed for the Azores. And we refueled in the Azores and fly to Newfoundland, Or Gander, and then from there we were to fly to Bath in northern Maine, and then down to Windsor Locks in Connecticut. Well, we took off the following morning. We got -- we took off very early. And instead of hitting a weather front, a storm front, the weather was beautiful. And as we were taking off, they couldn't close the bomb doors. They were stuck open. And the navigator lost his sextant, and I think the radio man went -- manually had to crank the bomb door shut, and we were distributed around the plane so that it would be -- the load would be distributed and he could fly straight. Well, he had trouble gaining altitude, and then he discovered -- the pilot discovered the back end was heavy, and he asked those who were furthest back to come up to the flight deck, and before we had been in the air an hour, all of us were on that flight deck, and it was so crowded that I got up in the turret, the turret seat, and the turret had been perforated with shells and it was so noisy. It was whistling. I couldn't hear what was going on below. But we got somewhere off the coast of, I think, Portugal. We were getting close to the Azores and we hit a storm, and the plane kept losing altitude and the sea was rough and we were down about 200 feet off the water. And everybody on that flight deck was milling around and they were starting to put parachutes on. I didn't even have a parachute. I left it in the back of the plane. And I heard the radio man say, "I am getting out of here." I think we had an engineer as well as the radio man, so there might have been a crew of five. Anyway, he said "I am getting out of here, I don't care", and he was ready to jump. And the outboard engine caught fire. Oil had been spraying out of the thing, and I thought to myself, well, we are going down, and I don't think there is any way we are going to survive this. I didn't even have a chute. And I thought how intelligent that colonel was. He knew what he was talking about. We should have listened to him. But in any case, it looked like we were just over the tops of the waves, and the wind had been picking up, and all of a sudden there was the Azores in front of us and we landed. We just got over whatever hills there were surrounding the airfield. And we went sailing down the runway with ambulances on both sides and fire engines, and we hardly got out of the plane and they were hosing it. Anyway, we stayed there for about three days while they shipped in a new engine from the states and replaced that engine and repaired the wing and did whatever they had to do and we took off again. But they had somehow been able to redistribute the loading on the plane or the weight distribution of the plane itself, and we flew, although the tail was low, the nose was up in the air, but not to the extent that it was when we got to the Azores, and we got to Newfoundland. But when we got there, the pilot complained that one of the engines was acting up and wanted a new engine, and we waited there for three days while we got another new engine. And when we finally landed at Windsorlocks, the plane had hit the ground and it was the end of the runway and we had to get off the plane right there and as we were getting off, the crew started dismantling the plane. They took everything out of the cabin that they could like oxygen bottles and anything that was lose they pulled out of there. And they were demolishing it as we left. And a truck picked us up and was taking us back to the base, and we noticed this mountain of wings and fuselages that they just threw in a huge pile to make room for other planes coming in. It was very busy. Anyway, we didn't even get a furlough, but we were taken by train to South Carolina where we entered a program to learn about the specific weather. We were going to be shipped to the Pacific and I think that course -- I think it was about three or four weeks after which we were given a 30 day furlough. And I came home for the 30 days. I think I was home about two weeks and the war ended with Japan, and I was so happy. I went back. I was given -- I got a telegram to report at Benjamin Harrison in Indiana and I would be discharged, and that is my story.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Would you have been part of the invasion of Japan?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Yes. Well, I don't know. We were taught -- we studied specific weather. (END OF FILE ONE. BEGINNING OF FILE TWO.)

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Yes. We would have been involved in whatever bombing they were doing at the island. They were building up the Pacific. At Benjamin Harrison, we came in contact with other Air Force people and even some infantrymen who were being shipped out of the Mediterranean. They were shipped from the Mediterranean. They weren't needed there any longer when the invasion was going on in Germany and they went through the Panama Canal and they were on their way into the Pacific as part of an invasion group, forces, and they had to turn around and go back to California. So it was just -- it was wonderful. I had been interviewed by a gal who asked -- she was in high school at the time, and they were studying, I guess, maybe the ethics of war or something like that, and she felt that it was immoral having used the atomic bomb in Japan and we caused so much suffering, and I mentioned to her that from my perspective, it prevented a lot of loss of the American lives. I think they thought we would lose a million or a million and a half men. It was quite impregnable. Anyway, that's my story.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Let's take you back a little bit. What was life like in Hawaii before the attack?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: It was wonderful. It was a wonderful place to be, the weather, the people. Although the island was so full, I guess it always had been -- has been a military base, and we were restricted. There were certain places we couldn't go. Uniformed men were not permitted in certain areas of Honolulu or even at Scofield where there were officers' quarters. And oddly enough, this guy, Jay Dolly, he was a lieutenant out of West Point, and he became our G-2 officer -- I think that was the term, the intelligence officer, and we were good friends. We were in the same calculus class, as a matter of fact, because we had an advanced math class. And he was a bright student, and I was doing well, and we were in that class together. And I knew his family, and when i went up to him, I said, "Jay". And he said, "I will talk to you later." He held me off. And he did. He invited me to dinner at his house and I met his wife. But we had very little to do with each other. That was -- he made me aware that we were still friends, but we could not fraternize.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You mentioned the one storage tank that was not hit. Did they suspect espionage had something to do with that?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Not espionage, but they had wonderful intelligence. And another sideline on that. We had shot down on the second raid, we had shot down a Japanese plane, and we were marched into the Naval Air Station and there was a rather comically shaped hill, and we were deployed around that hill. We had a couple machine guns, 30 caliber machine gun squads. I think we had four machine gun squads. One of them shot down a Japanese plane and it landed right at the base of this mountain, and the Marines went over there with an ambulance and pulled the guy out. It may not have been Marines. It could have been Naval men. But they pulled the pilot out. He was dead. And we heard afterwards that he wore civilian clothes under his flightsuit, and he wore an Ohio State sweater. So they were, I think that is against the Code of Ethics, whatever that is for wars, but he was, in the event he was shot down, he would be able to mix in with the population. And the other thing in line with that, the commander of the Naval Air Station refused to permit us to go back to Scofield. We were supposed to go back to Scofield and I don't know what all, to reorganize, but he kept us there, D Company, and refused to permit a group of National Guard soldiers who were marching to occupy -- I guess they might have been coast artillery men. He wouldn't let them on the reservation because he didn't trust -- the majority of the men were Japanese. And they were U. S. Soldiers. They were in the National Guard. And he refused to let them on base. And he set up a group of Marines with guns and wouldn't permit them on, and kept us there until -- well, I left in October of '43. I don't know what happened after that except that the 34th Engineers were converted to a combat regiment and became part of the 24th Division, the Pineapple Division, and they went island hopping in the Pacific, and I met after the war, about 1950 or '51, I met this fellow downtown and he was in the 34th with me. We were drafted together. And he said that of the 150 of us that went to Hawaii to form the 34th engineer, only 26 came back. They were just decimated. And that is an awful thing. Terrible. Anyway, when I was stationed in Scotland, we didn't get married, although I couldn't forget about her, and after the war we started correspondence and she came over here and we were married. And there is a group, Daughters of the British Empire, who are composed of immigrants to the U.S. after the war. So many Brits came here because of the hardships that existed in Britain and a good many of them married G.I.'S as war brides.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Getting back to Hawaii, was there a feeling of tension in Hawaii before the attack? Did you feel like it was a potential target?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Yes. Yes. Yes. I don't know why, but I think it was the Wednesday before the attack, there was an exercise on the island. It was some maneuver and the Coast Guard artillery or the artillery -- I don't know if it was just the coast, but the fuel artillery, too. I think artillery was dispersed all around the island. I think they had set up positions on beaches all around the island. And the Wednesday before it ended, they all went back into Fort Shafter, Fort DeRussy, all of them went back to their bases. And I remember coming in from Honolulu to Kailua and the road was just packed with trucks and guns and caissons. They were moving everything back to their base, and I thought, gee, I wonder why. Well, it was an exercise that they were training. There is always training measures going on. I mean, training exercises going on. We had maneuvers at one time, and because I was on the surveying squad, I got to know the island pretty well or sections of the island, and I was in a gun crew, an anti-tank gun crew. We carried a 37 millimeter gun behind a jeep, and I think there were four of us in the crew, and I was the leader of the squad on one gun. We had four of them. And we were involved in a maneuver, and I knew a place where we could be within the area we were responsible for, but it was high on top of a -- well, it was in the mountains, but it was up high and we overlooked a valley and there was a road right down the middle of the valley, and it was just outside of Honolulu, and I drove up there and took the gun off the truck or the jeep and set it on this bluff where it overlooked this valley and this road. And we sat down and started smoking cigarettes, and I think we ate lunch, and we were just kind of resting, and a group drove up, including a general, and he looked at our position and he looked down at the group of trucks moving in the valley, and he said, "What a wonderful situation. You have just killed -- you have just knocked out nine tanks." And this guy is writing everything down he is saying, and he said, "What outfit are you with?" And we told told him. And he said you are being credited with destroying nine enemy tanks and off they went and we didn't do a darn thing.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember what you were doing on Saturday, December 6?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Yes. I went to Honolulu. As a matter of fact, I took pictures. And I do have a snapshot showing on the way back to camp, somehow or other -- anyway, I took a snapshot of Pearl Harbor with all the battleships lined up beside Ford Island, and I was looking for it to take to the dinner on Saturday.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: That was taken on the 6th?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You can't find it?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: I came across a photograph of downtown Honolulu which was just crowded with servicemen because they were building up on the island. We were aware of new people always coming into Scofield, and they had built additional barracks and there was a lot going on. We were preparing for war.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you go to a club that day then, the 6th? Could you get into a club? Was it too crowded?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: It was crowded. Honolulu was crowded. It wasn't that day, but I think it was the first trip I ever made to Honolulu. I am walking down this street and approaching a bar that had glass windows in the front. It was a store. And somebody had thrown a sailor out through the door, and I had to stop because he would have hit me. And this sailor was moving out to the road. Somebody had thrown him through the door. FEMALE VOICE: Through the glass?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: No. The door was open. And I thought gee, whiz, what is going on, and I looked and Marines and sailors were fighting, and it was such a -- you know, for me to come across something like that, I was so naive, but the thing about it was I noticed there was a monkey sitting on the chandelier unscrewing lightbulbs and throwing it at the bar. And the lightbulbs were hitting this mirror, and I thought I wish I had a camera. It was so funny. And all these guys were punching each other and wrestling. And they called the MP's or the shore patrol, and I am standing there watching, and these guys rush in and they started hauling people into -- into this wagon. Anyway, years later I was working with a guy who had been the first Marine regimen and I was telling about this, and he said, Oh, that was our pet monkey. I was involved in that. He said they picked me up, but they released me the next morning. And I was so tickled to get that confirmed that I had really witnessed all of that. But Honolulu was a very busy place. And so many servicemen. FEMALE VOICE: And a correction, if I may say something. Before D-Day, we had troops from -- we had Italian prisoners. We had the Russian BD camp, plus all the men that were waiting to be involved in the invasion from God knows how many countries, and of course there was a similar situation. People were getting restless and becoming raucous, and my uncle was a prominent dentist in my home town, and so he had to go and identify by their dental records the people that fell victim to this kind of behavior. And so I think we had French. I will never never never forget them. It was wild. It was really really wild. a Yes. There was a problem with French sailors in Britain. They weren't being paid and they had no money, and they would be on leave, and what could they do. They couldn't buy anything, and we weren't -- when there was -- I know at one time a French frigate put in at this little town of Trune which was close to Prestwick. We weren't permitted in that town because those sailors would -- they knew G.I.'s had money and they would jump them and take the money. And some of them, we were told, they wore -- they carried a knife, like a dagger in there -- the back of their blouse. They wore middies, similar to the U.S. Navy. And they had a pocket back there and they could reach back there and pick up that knife and stick it at you and say, give me your money, and you had to turn it over, and sometimes if you refused, they were using a knife and you didn't have anything. Anyway, we weren't permitted into Trune. There was French sailors there. FEMALE VOICE: On the other hand, in my home town, the town arranged dances and whatnot for the servicemen that were in the area, and that, in fact, is where I spoke to this one French sailor who was from Champaign, and that is where I danced with a black man from the Canary Islands. And when he came up to me, I wasn't sure how to behave really. I mean, I didn't have any objection, and I did dance with him, but I never had any experience. The only dark skinned people we had in Britain, for the most part, were Indians, Asian Indians, but anyhow, he spoke beautiful English and he was from the Canary Islands.

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Talking about Indians, I had -- I had received a phone call from a cousin of mine who was in East Anglia. He was near Cambridge. He was a radio operator on a B-17 crew, 381 Bomber Group. They lost more planes and more men than any group in the U.S. Air Force. They were really -- they really suffered an awful lot, and he was very fortunate, he and -- there were three of them who returned to the states. They were the only three left of a crew of ten. When they had gone through their tour of duty and I think they went on like 35 missions, but that group was -- suffered an awful lot of damages. They were early on, and they were entering -- they were bombing Germany before we had the Thunderbird or the planes that could fly far enough, and the fighter planes that could protect them. Anyway, he had an awful experience, and right now he is in a hospital, a mental hospital, but he contacted me and I went down and we spent two days together. I was able to get off for two days, and it was quite an experience for me, and I wrote about it because he was writing a book, and it was a mess. As he finished a chapter, he sent it to me and asked me what I thought of it and it wasn't very good, but he had a story to tell. And he asked me to write to him from my point of view what had happened when I visited him at the Air Force base, and I did. And it was the funniest thing. I started to write to him. I didn't even know how to begin. And all of a sudden, the whole thing came to me and I just -- I couldn't write fast enough to get it out of my head. And I sent it to him, and I am not sure it was exactly what he wanted, and I don't know if he ever incorporated it, but I have a copy of it here.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you have an extra copy?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Yes, I made this copy for you.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Great. I can do something with that. Definitely.

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: I was leaving to go back to Prestwick, and he brought his pilot over to me. He was arranging a ride for me into Cambridge and the pilot came up and said to me if I wanted to go along, they were going on a practice flight, and I guess my cousin told him I washed out of cadets, and he said if you want to come with us, we have room for you, just get a parachute. And I did. And I went with them. And we were gone for about four hours. And they were flying over the North Sea and it was a practice mission to work out the logistics for the first thousand plane raid on Germany. By this time, they had the fighter plane escort. And I went up with them, and we were in pretty close formation, and you would look in any direction and that's all you saw was planes -- above you, below you. It just covered, really, I think, all of the North Sea. I think we saw the coast of Norway. Tremendous. And of course I had no idea that is what was going on, but when we -- it was an exercise. I knew that. And then the pilot told us, well, we'll be doing some more, he said. This is just the first, the start of attempting to work out how to get all these planes gathered together and then fly for some mission. It's frightening to see that many planes at one time. Anyway, that is in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Excellent. And when did you write this?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Oh, gosh. I don't have a date on it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Approximately, the year?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Oh, the year is in there.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You wrote this --

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: No, I wrote it about two years ago.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: One other quick question. Do you remember what was going through your mind when you actually knew you were under attack and for what purpose?

sp.speaker: Herbert Shure
sp.p: Yes. Yes. I had a strange experience before the war started. I was standing -- I was standing on a bluff overlooking the sea, the ocean. I was looking south from Ulu Po Heiau at the base of the volcano. Ulu Po Heiau was a volcano. The top was blown off it and you could see it. It landed in the sea about 20 miles away, and it was a typical frustrated cone, and before the war ended or before I had left that group, that volcano was almost completely hollowed out and became artillery emissions dump and not an observation, but an operating center for the coast artillery. Anyway, I was standing looking down at the beach and the body of a car was laying there. And the ocean, the waves, were just striking it and pulling back, striking it, and it was half buried in the sand, and I kept watching. I was almost hypnotized watching it. I must have been there for better than a half an hour and the sun was going down. It was almost dark. And I thought how wonderful the earth works, you know. Here man has taken from the soil or from the earth, all these minerals, had converted it into metals and built this car, and now the earth is claiming it back. It's drawing it back. And I felt that is what is going to happen to me. One day it's going to take all of my molecules and I would be nothing, but the earth would be replenished. And when the war started, I thought that was some sort of an omen or that is what is happening. I wouldn't -- like the first World War. I was born during the first World War. And like those who went off to war in 1916 or 1917, I won't come back. I won't. And when we were attacked, I thought I had a premonition, and I am not going to outlive this war. I never expected to. And when that engine caught on fire and we couldn't find our way, we couldn't hold altitude and we were on our way down to sea, I was ready for it. And I think the last -- for the last five minutes I kept thinking back on my whole life, that I was ready for it. I was ready to die. Well, when we were attacked, it seemed to me that I had anticipated something like that. You know, we were -- I was told by the draft board I would be in the service only for a year, and then released. And while I was at Belford in August, August of '41, Congress was debating extending the draft for another year. And I was sitting in the gallery at the House of Representatives on a weekend. I think it was on a Saturday. They had a session and they were arguing about the value or the need to extend the draft to two years, and every time someone would speak for it, the gallery was filled with servicemen. We would applaud. And they threatened to throw us out of there, but we took sides, and of course it passed, and we were to be there two years. But when December came around, I had only been in the service for six months. So five months. So that ended that. But, I think I was kind of surprised when I landed in the states and realized that I had been saved just going to the Pacific. And there is where I would hit my demise. And I think my mother suspected I was having a problem when I came home. I was here for 30 days. I think I was only home two weeks when the war ended in the Pacific, but you know, I did feel fear, but I didn't feel really courageous, as though I am going to become a hero. I just felt I was caught in a web. I felt I was caught in a web and that was life, and that was what the others had gone through. I remember responding to someone -- I can't remember the circumstances, but it occurred to me that we were such a disadvantaged generation. Those of us who were drafted into the Army in the early 40's, we were born for the most part during the first World War. And when we came to be teenagers, the first date I ever had -- I think it was the first date -- I had a quarter and I was taking my girlfriend to a movie, and I was only about 15 or 16 -- I think I was 16 -- and I hadn't gone to a movie very often. We weren't all that well off during the depression. And I thought the -- I thought the price of the movie was 10 cents, and I would have a nickel left over for a Mounds bar that we would split, and it turned out the movie was 15 cents. If you are over 14, you had to pay 15 cents, and I only had 25. The guy behind me gave me a nickel. It might have been his last nickel. But we were so disadvantaged, it just seemed to me, and here we are in the Golden Years, the 20's, and we are in uniform and there is a war going on. And what else can they throw at us? But that passed. I hadn't felt that we were -- I think we were blessed because the G.I. Bill of Rights, although I was in my third year at engineering school when I was drafted, when I came back, I could have gone anywhere, and I should have. I was towing with the idea of going to University of Chicago or one of the Ivy League schools. I could have gone anywhere. And I would have been paid 25 bucks a week to live on, stipend. But instead, I stayed here and couldn't get her out of my mind. But she came and we were married and that is in there, and my story about the eggs is in there as well.
